title: Tulsi (Ocimum tenuiflorum): Uses, Evidence & Safety | Ayurveda
metaDescription: Tulsi (Ocimum tenuiflorum), holy basil: traditional Ayurvedic use, what human trials show for stress and metabolism, and real safety cautions.
h1: Tulsi (Ocimum tenuiflorum): Traditional Use, Evidence and Cautions
answerCapsule: Tulsi (Ocimum tenuiflorum), or holy basil, is an aromatic herb revered in Ayurveda and Hindu tradition, taken as a tea, fresh leaf or extract. Small human trials, summarised in a 2017 systematic review, point to possible benefits for stress and some metabolic markers. Evidence is early and the trials are small. Tulsi is generally well tolerated but has cautions in pregnancy and around blood clotting.

sections.capsule: Tulsi (Sanskrit: tulasī; Ocimum tenuiflorum, synonym Ocimum sanctum), known in English as holy basil, is a fragrant shrub in the mint family and one of the most sacred plants in Hindu households. Ayurveda regards tulsi as a rasayana and often calls it an elixir herb, valuing it for the mind, breath and resilience to everyday stress.
sections.body:
Tulsi has been cultivated around Indian homes and temples for more than two thousand years, both as a devotional plant and a household remedy. Its Sanskrit name *tulasī* runs through the classical literature, and it is traditionally described as warming, light and drying — a profile Ayurveda links with kindling digestion and clearing the channels of the chest.

Botanically tulsi is *Ocimum tenuiflorum* (the older synonym *Ocimum sanctum* is still widely used); it is a close relative of culinary sweet basil but distinct in aroma and chemistry, owing to constituents such as eugenol and ursolic acid. Common types include the green Rama tulsi and the purple Krishna tulsi. In Ayurvedic terms it is most often used where [kapha and vata](/doshas) are involved, and it is usually taken as a hot-water infusion of the fresh or dried leaf. For how single herbs sit within the wider system, see the [herbs overview](/herbs).

sections.h2: What does the science say about tulsi?
sections.capsule: Tulsi is one of the more-researched Ayurvedic herbs for stress. A 2017 systematic review of 24 human trials reported benefits across stress, metabolic and immune measures, with no serious adverse events, but judged most trials small and short [1]. Several were placebo-controlled studies of a few weeks. Findings are encouraging rather than conclusive, and tulsi is studied for these uses, not proven to cure illness [3].
sections.body:
Tulsi has attracted more clinical study than many Ayurvedic herbs, though the evidence should be read with care.

A 2017 systematic review examined 24 human intervention studies and concluded that tulsi may benefit a range of stress, metabolic, cardiovascular and immune measures, and — importantly for safety — that no study reported a significant adverse event [1]. The catch is scale: most of those trials were small, ran for only a few weeks, used different tulsi preparations and doses, and several were open to bias, so the review called for larger and longer studies before firm clinical claims can be made.

The most consistent signal is for psychological stress: small placebo-controlled trials have reported lower self-rated stress and anxiety scores after six to eight weeks. A widely cited 2014 overview places these findings in the context of tulsi's long traditional use and its many active constituents, while being candid that mechanisms are not fully understood [3]. In short, tulsi is a promising, well-tolerated herb that is studied for stress and general wellbeing — not a proven cure for any diagnosed condition. For the bigger evidence question, see [is Ayurveda scientific?](/is-ayurveda-scientific).

sections.h2: What are the side effects and cautions of tulsi?
sections.capsule: Tulsi is generally well tolerated as a tea or food, with occasional mild nausea the main complaint. Because tulsi may affect blood sugar and can slow blood clotting, people on diabetes or anticoagulant medication should seek medical advice. Animal studies raise a possible effect on fertility, so tulsi is best avoided at medicinal doses in pregnancy and when trying to conceive.
sections.body:
The specific cautions worth knowing:

- **Blood sugar:** tulsi may lower blood glucose, which is one of the metabolic effects noted in human trials [1]. If you take medication for diabetes, monitor your levels, because doses may need review.
- **Blood clotting:** tulsi can slow clotting and may add to the effect of anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs; caution is sensible around warfarin or aspirin, and stop tulsi before planned surgery.
- **Pregnancy, breastfeeding and fertility:** animal studies have suggested tulsi may reduce fertility and is best not taken at medicinal doses in pregnancy; culinary amounts in food are a different matter, but concentrated supplements should be avoided when pregnant, breastfeeding or trying to conceive.
- **Thyroid:** high intakes have been reported to influence thyroid hormone levels in animals, so use care if you have a thyroid condition.
- **Contamination:** heavy-metal risk in any Ayurvedic product reflects manufacturing quality, not the plant itself [2]. Choose a maker that follows a recognised Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standard with heavy-metal testing.

These are practical cautions and interactions, not a suggestion that tulsi treats any disease.

sections.h2: Where can I find quality tulsi?
sections.capsule: Tulsi is widely sold as loose-leaf tea, dried powder, capsules and standardised extracts, and quality is uneven. Because any herbal supplement can carry contaminants, choose tulsi from a maker that follows a recognised Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standard with heavy-metal testing and clear species labelling. Where tulsi is used within care, a qualified physician prescribes it at an NABH-accredited Ayurvedic hospital.
sections.body:
Tulsi grown and processed under a recognised **Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standard**, with correct botanical identification and heavy-metal testing, answers the contamination concern documented across the wider herbal market [2]. That is a quality-control statement, not a claim that tulsi is a treatment for any illness.

If you want to use tulsi beyond an occasional cup of tea, a qualified Ayurvedic physician can advise whether it fits your constitution and your current medicines. To compare tulsi with other well-studied herbs, read about [amla](/herbs/amla), [ashwagandha](/herbs/ashwagandha), [brahmi](/herbs/brahmi), [triphala](/herbs/triphala) and [turmeric](/herbs/turmeric); supervised [panchakarma](/panchakarma) is one setting where herbs are given under guidance.

faqs.q: Does tulsi help with stress and anxiety?
faqs.a: Several small placebo-controlled trials, pulled together in a 2017 systematic review, found that tulsi extracts lowered self-rated stress and anxiety scores over six to eight weeks, with a good safety record. The trials were small and short, so tulsi is best viewed as a possible support for everyday stress rather than a proven treatment for an anxiety disorder. Persistent anxiety deserves professional assessment.

faqs.q: Is tulsi safe to drink every day?
faqs.a: For most healthy adults, a daily cup or two of tulsi tea is generally well tolerated and is a long-standing everyday habit in India. Concentrated capsules and extracts are a different matter: they may affect blood sugar and blood clotting, and are best avoided in pregnancy. If you take regular medication or are trying to conceive, check with a doctor before using strong supplements.

faqs.q: What is the difference between tulsi and ordinary basil?
faqs.a: Tulsi (Ocimum tenuiflorum, or holy basil) is a distinct species from the sweet basil used in cooking (Ocimum basilicum). They share the mint family but differ in aroma and active compounds — tulsi is richer in eugenol and ursolic acid, and is grown chiefly as a medicinal and sacred plant rather than a kitchen herb. Check the Latin name so you know which one you are buying.

No. Tulsi is studied for stress and some metabolic markers, but the trials are small and it is not a proven substitute for any prescribed medicine. Never stop or replace medication for a diagnosed condition on your own. If you would like to add tulsi alongside conventional care, discuss it with your doctor first, especially if you take drugs for diabetes or blood thinning.
